subject: Biology
title: Genes and Chromosomes
description: A short lesson to help you apply Genes and Chromosomes.

hook.text: A gene is a stretch of DNA that codes for one protein. Humans have about 20,000 genes.

buildup.text: Genes sit on chromosomes—long, tightly coiled DNA bundles. Humans have 23 pairs.

discovery.text: You get one set of 23 chromosomes from your mother and one set from your father.

twist.text: Genes make up only about 2% of your DNA. The rest was once dismissed as 'junk.'

climax.text: Scientists now know much of that non-coding DNA regulates when and how genes turn on.

punchline.text: Twenty thousand genes. Three billion letters.

quiz.question: How many chromosome pairs do humans have?

details.summary: Genes are segments of DNA that encode instructions for proteins or functional RNA molecules. They are organized on chromosomes, long DNA molecules packaged with histone proteins. Humans have about 20,000 protein-coding genes distributed across 23 pairs of chromosomes.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding genes and chromosomes is foundational to all of genetics. Knowing how genes are organized, inherited, and expressed explains hereditary disease, physical traits, and the biological diversity of all living things.
takeaways: Humans have approximately 20,000 protein-coding genes on 23 chromosome pairs
Genes occupy specific locations called loci on chromosomes
Chromosomes are visible during cell division as X-shaped structures

faq.question: Why do humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes?
faq.answer: You inherit one set of 23 from each parent, totaling 46 chromosomes. The paired arrangement ensures you have two copies of nearly every gene, providing backup if one copy is damaged and enabling genetic diversity through sexual reproduction.

faq.question: Does having more genes make an organism more complex?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Rice has about 38,000 genes compared to our 20,000. Complexity comes more from gene regulation, alternative splicing, and protein interactions than from gene number alone. How genes are used matters more than how many exist.
